meta.title: ADW ecosystem hook integration
meta.goal: Integrate all 51 validated ADW-scoped ecosystem hook ideas into agent-discipline-watcher: 38 built across ten epics, 13 explicitly deferred with reasons. ADW stays a deterministic, blocking-or-injecting discipline layer across its four clients (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi).
meta.strategy: TDD per task on the existing 86-test pytest net, staged Lean rollout for every new blocking gate (observe-first per D7, promoted on adjudicated ledger evidence), with DevOps and responsible-engineering gates borrowed where a hook touches install, user prompts, or secrets.
meta.strategy_rationale: Hook code is logic-heavy and bug-prone, so the delivery strategy is test-first. The real product risk is not code correctness but gate behavior in live sessions: a false-blocking Stop hook is worse than no hook. So the riskiest assumption is tested by the smallest slice (dispatcher plus Stop gate, live-verified) before the wide build-out, and every new gate ships in observe until the adjudicated ledger shows its precision.
meta.first_slice: E1 foundation plus E2-S1-T1 Stop gate plus E2-W-T0 Stop-only wiring, live-verified by the E10-T0 smoke and measured by the findings ledger (E1-S1-T4).
meta.round_trip: architect-plan.json is the single source of truth. The human edits plan.html and exports JSON, and the architect regenerates plan.html and agent-plan.md from the edited JSON. This is a file round-trip, not a live server.
release_trains: R1 foundation plus Stop smoke: E1, E2-S1, E2-W-T0, E10-T0. Nothing else wires live before E10-T0 passes.
R2 event and parity hardening: the rest of E2, E3, E4, E5, the adapter tasks, E10-T1.
R5 telemetry and negative memory: E8, E9, then E10-T2 and E10-T3.
execution_waves: Wave 1 (parallel): E1-S1-T1 | E1-S1-T2 | E1-S1-T3 (disjoint files, no dependencies), then E1-S1-T4 (needs the session-state store for turn-id stamping), then E1-S1-T5 (needs the state store and the ledger for its transition rows).

Wave 2 (parallel): E1-S2-T1 then E1-S2-T2 | E2-S1-T1 | E2-S2-T1 | E2-S3-T1 | E2-S4-T1 | E2-S5-T1 | E3-S1-T1 | E4-S2-T1 | E5-S1-T1 | E6-S1-T1 | E7-S1-T1 | E8-S1-T1 | E9-S2-T1 | E9-S3-T1 (all owned_paths disjoint).

Wave 3 (mixed): the pre_write.py chain is strictly sequential (E3-S2-T1 -> E4-S1-T1 -> E4-S3-T1 -> E4-S4-T1 -> E4-S5-T1 -> E8-S1-T4). The stop.py chain is E2-S1-T1 -> E2-S1-T2 -> E8-S1-T2 -> E6-W-T1. The prompt_submit.py chain runs E3-S1-T2 -> E3-S1-T3 -> E8-S1-T3. E6 recipes (S2 to S8) run parallel to each other and to the E7-S2 chain. E5-S2-T1 fits anywhere here.

Gate between waves: E2-W-T0 wires the Stop hook alone and E10-T0 smokes it live. Every further wiring task sits behind E10-T0 in the graph, so the broad rollout cannot start before the event bet is proven. Implementation tasks (code plus tests, nothing live) may proceed meanwhile.

Wave 4 (sequential on shared wiring files, all behind E10-T0): E2-W-T1 -> E3-W -> E4-W -> E5-W -> E6-W (after E8-S1-T2 for stop.py) -> E9-W, then E9-S1-T1 (dead-rules integrations, after E8-W-T1 for session_end.py and E7-S2-T3 for record.py) and the E10 rollout tasks. E2-W-T2 (OpenCode adapter) and E2-W-T3 (Pi adapter) own only their adapter files and run parallel to this chain.

research.question: What does ADW wire today?
research.finding: PreToolUse on edits (pre_write.py) and Bash pre-commit (pre_commit.py), PostToolUse on edits (record.py), SessionStart with matcher startup|resume|clear|compact (session_start.py). run.sh already accepts a Stop event and exits 0. The scanner is one canonical Python lib (hooks/lib/scanner.py, three families) behind thin client adapters (Claude snippet, Codex TOML, OpenCode TS plugin, Pi extension). 86 tests pass via 'cd hooks && python3 -m pytest -q'.
research.source: repo read: hooks/run.sh, hooks/*.py, hooks/lib/*, claude-settings.snippet.json, codex-config.snippet.toml, install.sh, test run 2026-07-24

research.question: Is SessionStart(compact) re-injection new work?
research.finding: No. Both the Claude snippet and the Codex TOML already match 'compact'. The gap is that session_start.py injects one generic line for every source. The compact path needs the full contract plus the restored snapshot, so E5 is an enrichment, not new wiring.
research.source: repo read: claude-settings.snippet.json line 36, codex-config.snippet.toml line 2

research.question: Do the cited new hook events exist with the claimed payloads?
research.finding: Trusted per lead decision: the validator confirmed Stop, SubagentStop, UserPromptSubmit, ConfigChange, PreCompact, PostToolBatch, PostToolUseFailure, TaskCompleted, SessionEnd, InstructionsLoaded, the if field, and async:true against the official hooks reference (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks and hooks-guide). Not independently re-verified here, and no client version is pinned in the citation. Containment instead of re-verification: all schema knowledge in lib/payloads.py, a per-event fallback column in the parity matrix, the E10-T0 live Stop smoke gating all further wiring, and the E10 smokes recording the installed client version next to their results.
research.source: lead decision plus outputs/adw-scoped-ideas.md correction notes

research.question: Which events exist on Codex, OpenCode, and Pi?
research.finding: Assumed unknown beyond what the current adapters use (SessionStart, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop in the OpenCode type union). E1-S2-T2 produces the parity matrix from each client's primary docs. Gates degrade to Claude-only where an event is missing, documented per gate.
research.source: assumption, plus repo read: opencode/agent-discipline-watcher.ts WatcherEvent type

research.question: Does ADW's pre-commit gate already scan the staged snapshot?
research.finding: Yes: pre_commit.py reads staged content via 'git show :path', not the working tree. This weakens the case for the exact-snapshot worktree and OID-certificate proposal and supports deferring it.

research.question: What can the OpenCode and Pi adapter shims actually express?
research.finding: ADW is a four-client repo: install.sh wires --claude, --codex, --opencode, and --pi on by default. The OpenCode plugin listens only on tool.execute.before/after for write tools, session.created, and session.idle (a pseudo-Stop that injects a chat system message, not a real block). The Pi extension listens only on before_agent_start and tool_result, which is post-hoc: it scans after the write and reports isError, with no pre-execution block point and no Bash or git-commit coverage. Wiring a new event to these clients therefore means extending the shim itself first, and some blocking gates are structurally out of reach on Pi today.
research.source: critic-adw repo read of opencode/agent-discipline-watcher.ts and pi/extensions/agent-discipline-watcher/index.ts, corroborated by the WatcherEvent type union

research.question: Does the Codex merge tooling survive new event names?
research.finding: No, not by itself: hooks/merge-codex-config.py hardcodes HOOK_LIFECYCLES = {PreCompact, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionEnd, SessionStart, Stop, UserPromptSubmit} for stripping stale hook blocks. Wiring SubagentStop, PostToolBatch, TaskCompleted, PostToolUseFailure, InstructionsLoaded, or ConfigChange into codex-config.snippet.toml without extending that allow-list makes the strip logic silently mishandle those blocks on reinstall. E1-S2-T2 carries this as an explicit deliverable.

decisions.choice: Keep one canonical Python engine (hooks/lib) behind thin per-client adapters. No HTTP service, no MCP server, no daemon. The type:http and mcp_tool hook types are deferred.
decisions.tradeoff: Per-client adapters must be extended by hand for each new event, but ADW gains no network dependency, no auth surface, and no daemon lifecycle to babysit.

decisions.choice: All event-schema knowledge lives in one payload-normalization module (hooks/lib/payloads.py) with contract tests per documented field. Hooks never read raw payload keys directly.
decisions.tradeoff: One extra indirection per hook, but schema drift across Claude Code versions breaks one tested file instead of eleven hooks.

decisions.choice: Every hook lands with a test in the hooks/test_*.py pattern plus the full pytest gate. Wiring tasks additionally re-run merge-config tests. A small live end-to-end verification (E10-T1) proves acceptance behavior without replacing focused tests.
decisions.tradeoff: More test code to maintain than ad-hoc hook scripts, in exchange for regression evidence on every change.

decisions.choice: Session-scoped state (freeze lease, first-touch acks, failure streaks, dead ends, compaction snapshot) is durable JSON on disk under ~/.agent-discipline/state/<session_id>/, written atomically, cleaned by SessionEnd.
decisions.tradeoff: State files need lifecycle management, but gates survive crash, compaction, and hook-process restarts, which in-memory state cannot.

decisions.choice: Work splits by hook event and capability (delivery slices), not by technical layer. Contended files (pre_write.py, stop.py, prompt_submit.py, the snippets) get explicit sequential dependency chains so no two open tasks own the same file.
decisions.tradeoff: Some cross-epic dependencies (the verify lib feeds E2), but zero merge collisions between parallel workers.

decisions.choice: Stdlib-only Python 3.11+, matching the existing codebase. Atomic file replacement and locking follow CPython primary-documented behavior (os.replace, fcntl).
decisions.tradeoff: No third-party ergonomics, in exchange for a zero-dependency install on all clients.

decisions.choice: Every gate has three states in central config: off, observe, and enforce. New gates ship in observe, where the full check runs and the ledger records a would_block row but nothing blocks. The metric is fully producible: every entry script runs through the shared main wrapper, which emits one observed heartbeat row per invocation and stamps every ledger row with the session's current turn_id from session state, stop.py advances that turn counter on the first Stop of a turn only, never on a stop_hook_active retry after a block (the pseudo-Stop equivalent advances it on clients without Stop per the parity matrix, and a family with no turn producer on its client is reported per-invocation and labeled as such), so the denominator is the count of distinct observed turn_ids, never raw invocations, which a multi-fire hook would inflate. lib/config logs a state-transition row whenever a family's effective state changes (the producer for the override signal), and the observe report renders each family's would_block sample for the weekly review, persists the lead's true-or-false-signal labels as adjudication rows in the ledger (the adjudication that would_block incidence alone cannot supply), and computes the per-family adjudicated false-signal rate per 20 observed turns, the number E10-T2 consumes. Promotion to enforce requires a burn-in window of at least one week and an adjudicated false-signal rate at or under 1 per 20 observed turns for that family, decided at E10-T2. The existing three families keep their current enforce defaults. No exceptions among shipped gates: the TaskCompleted scan, the taint self-protection rule, and the commit-message scan also start in observe. Explicit opt-in features (freeze lease, first-touch gate, at-mention rule, the injection maps, the data_boundary tier) are user-invoked, not silently shipped, so they enforce on enable, and their default-off wording refers to the feature switch, not a gate state.
decisions.tradeoff: Slower protection rollout and a weekly adjudication chore for the lead, but the false-block metric has a defined producer for every term before enforcement, and rollback is a config flip.

decisions.choice: Defer all non-deterministic hook types (type:prompt, type:agent, the LLM-judge Stop gate, prompt/agent SubagentStop QA): they break ADW's deterministic-blocking contract, and agent hooks are documented as experimental.
decisions.tradeoff: Judgment-call rules (hollow test versus trivial test) stay regex-approximate, but every block stays reproducible and explainable.

decisions.choice: The UserPromptSubmit firewall defaults to injecting a warning, not blocking, on matched human prompts. Block-mode is an explicit config opt-in.
decisions.tradeoff: A user can still push past the warning, but ADW never silently erases a human's prompt by default, which is the higher harm.

decisions.choice: Blocking parity is capability-bounded per adapter, never assumed. Pi's adapter has no pre-execution hook point, so blocking gates degrade to post-hoc findings on Pi. OpenCode's pseudo-Stop is injection-only. A gate task for a both-scoped idea is complete only when the parity matrix row records per-client status (wired, degraded, or not available), and touching only Claude wiring never marks such an idea done.
decisions.tradeoff: Honest degraded parity is documented instead of pretended uniform enforcement, at the cost of a per-gate matrix row to maintain.

decisions.choice: One entry script per event-and-matcher pair, never two hooks racing on the same surface. Where several capabilities share a surface they compose inside the entry script in a fixed order: input rewrites first, then structural gates, then content scans, first deny wins, injected contexts concatenate. Concretely: pre_write.py orchestrates the edit-PreToolUse pipeline (redaction rewrite, protected, freeze, first-touch, taint, scan), record.py orchestrates PostToolUse (edit journal, scan, verify recipes, spill, output redaction), and pre_commit.py and pre_mcp.py own their disjoint matchers. Redaction and the formatter therefore land as lib modules called from these orchestrators, not as separate hooks.
decisions.tradeoff: The orchestrator files grow and their ownership chains get longer, but handler order and merge semantics are code, not an unspecified property of client hook dispatch.

decisions.choice: Command-bearing config is honored only after a user-owned trust grant recorded outside the repo (~/.agent-discipline/trust/<repo-fingerprint>), written by the installed CLI: 'agent-discipline trust' run in the repo, which works from any cwd because install.sh already links bin/agent-discipline into ~/.local/bin. Without the grant, verify, formatter, lint, typecheck, test, coverage, and AST recipes no-op with a visible note. Commands execute as argv lists, never through a shell. An end-to-end test proves the grant flow (trust, revoke, moved repo) from a temporary target repo after a sandbox install.
decisions.tradeoff: One extra explicit step per repo before quality gates run, in exchange for a checked-in .agent-discipline.json in an untrusted repo never executing code automatically.

decisions.choice: record.py's per-call scan is canonical and never suppressed. PostToolBatch is additive only: it reads the ledger rows already written for the batch and reports only new cross-file findings, so nothing is buffered and nothing is lost if PostToolBatch never fires. Correlation uses the per-call tool_use_id, carried in the payload contract and stored in every PostToolUse ledger row, matched against the ids in the PostToolBatch tool_calls array. If the live payloads lack the id (the contract test and the E10 smoke check for it), batch.py drops ledger dedupe entirely and restricts itself to intrinsically cross-file rules, its documented degraded mode.
decisions.tradeoff: A batch can surface two block messages (per-call plus cross-file) instead of one perfectly merged report, but no finding ever depends on an event that might not exist or a correlation field that might not arrive.

decisions.choice: Fail-safe registration: an unknown event key in a client config is treated as able to break config parsing before any handler runs, never assumed to be a dormant no-op. Therefore events register train by train behind the E10-T0 gate, every wiring task proves the merged config in a sandbox HOME (parse-back plus the client's own config validation where one exists) before the lead installs live, the parity matrix records the minimum client version per event, and the timestamped install backups are the immediate rollback when a client still rejects a key.
decisions.tradeoff: Wiring lands in more, smaller steps than one bulk registration, but a client that chokes on a new event key is caught in a throwaway HOME, not in the operator's live config.

validation.riskiest_assumption: The new hook events fire with the documented payload fields and honor blocking semantics in live sessions (trusted from the validator per lead decision, not re-verified), and a deterministic Stop-time gate blocks with high enough precision that users keep it enabled.
validation.mvp_slice: E1 (dispatcher, session state, payload contracts, ledger plus edit journal, config schema) plus E2-S1-T1 (Stop discipline gate) plus E2-W-T0 (Stop-only wiring) plus E10-T0 (live Stop smoke). Every further wiring task depends on E10-T0 in the graph, so the event bet is proven before the broad rollout can start.
validation.metric: From the JSONL ledger: would_block rows per 20 observed turns (distinct heartbeat turn_ids, advanced by stop.py per D7) while a family is in observe, the lead's true-or-false adjudication rows persisted by the observe report's adjudicate subcommand, block rows once enforcing, and the override signal (a state-transition row flipping a family off within the same session after a block). The observe report computes the per-family adjudicated false-signal rate E10-T2 consumes, so the false-block rate is computable before and after enforcement.
validation.decision_rule: E10-T0 first: if the Stop event does not fire or block as documented, stop and replan the turn-end epic before any further wiring. Then per family at E10-T2: a false-signal rate over 1 per 20 turns in a one-week observe window means the family stays in observe (or pivots to inject-only) and its rules get reworked. At or under threshold, promote to enforce.

epics.title: Foundation: dispatcher, state, payload contracts, ledger
epics.outcome: Every later hook plugs into a data-driven dispatcher, a tested payload layer, durable session state, and a findings ledger. Nothing user-visible changes yet except if-field scoping and async flags on existing wiring.

stories.title: Core libraries: dispatch, payloads, and gate config
stories.user_story: As the ADW maintainer, I want one dispatch table, one payload contract, one state store, and one ledger, so that eleven new hooks share tested plumbing instead of reinventing it.
acceptance_criteria: run.sh routes events from a single data-driven table, one entry script per event-and-matcher pair (D11), and unknown events still exit 2 with usage

lib/payloads.py exposes typed accessors for every documented field the plan consumes (session_id, cwd, tool_name, last_assistant_message, stop_hook_active, agent_id, agent_type, agent_transcript_path, prompt, source, file_path, error, is_interrupt, duration_ms, tool_calls, task_id, task_subject), each with a contract test
lib/config.py carries the central gate-state schema: every gate family resolves to off, observe, or enforce, with observe running the full check and writing would_block rows without blocking (D7)

every new hook module follows the existing pattern: an importable module exposing run(payload, config) with I/O only via the hookio helpers, so test files import it directly and call run() the way test_hooks.py already does

tasks.title: E1-S1-T1: Data-driven run.sh dispatcher
tasks.detail: Refactor the run.sh if-chain into a table (event to script) iterated in POSIX sh, preserving current routes (SessionStart, PreToolUse, PreCommit, PostToolUse, Stop no-op) and exit-2 usage on unknown events. New events are added later as one table line each. Documents D11: one entry script per event-and-matcher pair, composition happens inside the script (rewrites, then gates, then scans, first deny wins, contexts concatenate), never across racing hook registrations. Marked done on committed, tested work whose named checks pass. The paired critic produced concrete findings that changed the code but never returned a formal verdict, so the craft gate was closed by orchestrator verification instead: mutation checks that prove each new test fails when its logic breaks.
tasks.risk: POSIX sh portability across macOS and Linux, covered by a test invoking run.sh directly.

tasks.title: E1-S1-T3: Payload contract module (lib/payloads.py)
tasks.detail: Single module normalizing every hook event payload this plan consumes into plain dicts, including the routing context every hook needs (session_id, cwd, tool_name, and tool_use_id where the event documents it) and tolerant of the tool_input, toolInput, and input aliases pre_write already handles. Contract tests encode the documented schemas verbatim so a Claude Code schema change fails exactly here. Marked done on committed, tested work whose named checks pass. The paired critic produced concrete findings that changed the code but never returned a formal verdict, so the craft gate was closed by orchestrator verification instead: mutation checks that prove each new test fails when its logic breaks.
tasks.risk: Carries the plan's residual event-schema risk by design (risks[0]). That is its job.

tasks.title: E1-S1-T5: Central gate-state config schema (lib/config.py)
tasks.detail: Extend lib/config.py with the three-state gate model from D7: every gate family resolves to off, observe, or enforce, with helpers the hooks call to decide whether a finding blocks or lands as would_block. On resolution it compares each family's effective state to the last snapshot in session state and logs a state-transition ledger row on change, the defined producer for the override signal. Includes the schema for verify categories, data_boundary, and per-family kill-switches, so config keys are defined once. Closed on committed, tested work whose named checks pass, with the critic's PASS independently reproduced. One defect was caught after that PASS and fixed before shipping: the transition logger's lazy imports used bare module names, which resolve when a test imports config directly but not when a hook imports it as lib.config, and the broad except swallowed the ImportError, so the override signal would have been silently dead in production while its tests stayed green. A subprocess test now drives the real lib.config path.
tasks.risk: Schema creep. The task defines only the keys tasks in this plan consume, nothing speculative.

stories.title: Core libraries: durable session state and findings ledger
stories.user_story: As the ADW maintainer, I want one dispatch table, one payload contract, one state store, and one ledger, so that eleven new hooks share tested plumbing instead of reinventing it.
acceptance_criteria: lib/session_state.py survives process restart and concurrent writers (atomic replace), keyed by session_id, and offers a sweep API that removes stale session dirs, the janitor for a missed SessionEnd

every gate decision appends one JSONL ledger row with hook, rule, duration_ms, tool_use_id where present, and an outcome from the enum block, inject, would_block, no_edits, and record.py journals every successful edit (path, tool, ts) so completion gates know what changed this session
every entry script runs through the shared main wrapper, which emits one observed heartbeat row per invocation, the denominator for the D7 metric and the producer for the E10-T1 heartbeat check

tasks.title: E1-S1-T2: Durable session state store (lib/session_state.py)
tasks.detail: JSON state under ~/.agent-discipline/state/<session_id>/ with atomic os.replace writes, a read-modify-write helper, an explicit cleanup API called by SessionEnd, and a sweep_stale API that removes session dirs older than a configured age, the janitor for sessions whose SessionEnd never fired. Consumers: freeze lease, first-touch gate, failure streaks, dead ends, compaction snapshot. Marked done on committed, tested work whose named checks pass. The paired critic produced concrete findings that changed the code but never returned a formal verdict, so the craft gate was closed by orchestrator verification instead: mutation checks that prove each new test fails when its logic breaks. Accepted limit recorded here rather than in the module, because the repo's own scanner rejects narration in a docstring: the containment check and the write that follows it are separate syscalls, so a symlink swapped in between them would still escape. Planting one needs write access to the state root inside the user's own home, and an attacker holding that has already won without needing the race, so no O_NOFOLLOW reopen dance was added for it.
tasks.risk: Concurrent hook invocations racing on one file, mitigated by atomic replace plus an fcntl lock in the read-modify-write helper.

tasks.title: E1-S1-T4: Findings ledger, session edit journal, heartbeat wrapper, observe report
tasks.detail: Extend reporting.py with four producers. One: every gate decision writes one JSONL row (ts, session_id, hook, event, family, rule, path, tool_use_id where present, turn_id, outcome, duration_ms) under ~/.agent-discipline/ledger/, outcome one of block, inject, would_block, no_edits, release. Two: a shared main wrapper that every entry script uses, emitting one observed heartbeat row per invocation and stamping every row with the current turn_id read via lib/session_state (advanced by stop.py at turn end, D7), the E10 heartbeat producer. The count of distinct turn_ids is the metric denominator. Three: record.py journals every successful edit (path, tool, ts), the data model the Stop verify and TaskCompleted gates consume, in its own new test file. Four: an observe-report CLI in reporting.py (cd hooks && python3 -m lib.reporting observe-report) that lists a family's would_block rows for the weekly adjudication, persists the lead's true-or-false labels as adjudication rows via its adjudicate subcommand, and computes the per-family adjudicated false-signal rate per 20 distinct observed turn_ids, the number E10-T2 consumes (D7), all covered by pytest. compact_block behavior stays unchanged. Closed on committed, tested work whose named checks pass. record.py, the only entry script this task owns, routes through run_with_ledger, so PostToolUse contributes its observed heartbeat and bypassing the wrapper fails three tests. The remaining entry scripts, session_start.py, pre_write.py, and pre_commit.py, are not owned here and are wired through the wrapper by the E2 and E6 wiring tasks. E10-T2 must not read a false-signal rate until those land, because the denominator stays partial until then.
tasks.risk: Ledger writes must never block or fail a hook. Append errors are swallowed with a stderr note. Heartbeat rows are one line each so volume stays trivial.

stories.title: Existing-wiring hardening and parity map
stories.user_story: As the ADW maintainer, I want the existing wiring scoped tighter and a per-client event availability matrix, so that new-event wiring tasks have a factual basis per client.
acceptance_criteria: the Claude snippet's Bash pre-commit hook carries the documented if filter for git commit while pre_commit.py's own parser stays as the cross-client backstop
an async-flag policy exists: log-only hooks declare async true in the Claude snippet

a parity matrix (README section) states, per client and per event used in this plan, wired or degraded or not-available, from each client's primary docs, including the Pi post-hoc-only and OpenCode injection-only-Stop limits
HOOK_LIFECYCLES in merge-codex-config.py lists every event ADW wires, with a merge test asserting the list matches the snippet

tasks.title: E1-S2-T1: if-field scoping plus async flag policy on the Claude snippet
tasks.detail: Add the documented if filter to the Bash pre-commit entry and define the async:true convention for log-only hooks. Matchers otherwise unchanged. Closed with two lead-verified interpretations. The if literal is Bash(git commit *) with the word-boundary space, verified against the official permissions doc; the no-space form also matches git commit-tree and was rejected in review. The async policy ships blocker-side only: every current snippet entry is deny-capable or output-dependent, so the merge test asserts key absence of both async and asyncRewake on all watcher entries. The positive half (log-only hooks must declare async:true) lands with E9 wiring when the first log-only hook exists.
tasks.risk: The if syntax must match the documented permission-rule grammar exactly. The merge-config test asserts the literal.
ideas: if-field scoping to cut false-positive hook spawns

tasks.title: E1-S2-T2: Cross-client event parity matrix plus merge-script generalization
tasks.detail: Research, from primary docs per client, which of the new events exist on Codex, OpenCode, and Pi. Write the matrix into README.md, including the known adapter limits: OpenCode's pseudo-Stop is injection-only, and Pi has no pre-execution hook point so blocking gates degrade to post-hoc findings there (D10). Every event row also carries a fallback column stating what ADW does when that event never fires (for example Stop falls back to per-edit record.py scanning, UserPromptSubmit to the SessionStart contract injection, SessionEnd to the startup janitor sweep), and a minimum-client-version column per D14, since an unknown event key can break config parsing rather than no-op. Generalize the three merge scripts to merge arbitrary event keys idempotently, which explicitly includes extending HOOK_LIFECYCLES in merge-codex-config.py to every event ADW wires (SubagentStop, PostToolBatch, TaskCompleted, PostToolUseFailure, InstructionsLoaded, ConfigChange) so the stale-strip logic does not mishandle them on reinstall. Closed with two research corrections to plan premises. Current Pi documents a blocking pre-execution tool_call event, so D10's 'no pre-execution hook point' wording is stale; the ADW Pi adapter stays post-hoc and unwired, and whether to wire tool_call is an owner decision affecting E2-W-T3. Codex fires PostToolUse after failed Bash calls, so Codex failure coverage is degraded, not absent. No client publishes per-event minimum versions, so that column is uniformly unknown with the D14 sandbox-parse note.
tasks.risk: Codex and Pi docs may be thin. Where undocumented, the matrix says unknown and the gate ships Claude-only. A missed HOOK_LIFECYCLES entry silently corrupts reinstall merges, so the merge tests assert one entry per wired event.

epics.title: Turn-end and completion enforcement (Stop family)
epics.outcome: ADW can refuse to end a turn, a subagent, a task, or a tool batch while discipline findings or failed verification stand. This is the MVP value epic.

stories.title: Stop gate
stories.user_story: As an operator, I want the turn blocked when the final message claims done without evidence or violates prose discipline, so that unproved claims never end a turn silently.
acceptance_criteria: stop.py scans last_assistant_message with the existing scanner families plus an unproved-done rule in lib/done_claims.py (done, fixed, complete, or passing language with no verification evidence in the message), keeping scanner.py untouched
stop_hook_active is honored with no re-block loops, and the documented cap of eight consecutive blocks is respected by design
the optional verify mode runs trusted repo-declared commands, ships in observe per D7, and blocks on failure only once the family is promoted to enforce
every decision lands in the ledger

tasks.title: E2-S1-T1: stop.py discipline plus unproved-done gate
tasks.detail: New hooks/stop.py: read the Stop payload via lib/payloads, scan last_assistant_message with the existing scanner families plus a new deterministic unproved-done rule that lives in its own module lib/done_claims.py (scanner.py stays untouched, so E7-S1-T1 keeps sole ownership of it and both tasks stay parallel). Resolve the stop family's gate state through lib/config (D7), return a block decision with reason when enforcing and a would_block ledger row when observing, honor stop_hook_active, write ledger rows, and advance the session turn counter in lib/session_state only when stop_hook_active is false, so a blocked turn's stop_hook_active retries keep the same turn_id and the turn counts once, the producer for D7's turn denominator with the retry dedupe as an explicit test case. A Stop invocation that arrives with stop_hook_active true and passes the gate writes a ledger row with outcome release, the explicit marker the E10-T0 smoke asserts, and by construction that row can only follow a block in the same session. Replaces the run.sh Stop no-op. Closed after four critic rounds. Two design upgrades landed beyond the letter of the spec: release rows require a state-proved pending-block marker in session state, not the client-asserted stop_hook_active flag, and evidence means shown results only, never tool mentions, which removes the negation-phrasing attack surface by deletion. Quote stripping uses line-local odd/even pairing with an over-strip ban and a documented malformed-quote trade-off.
tasks.risk: Scanning final prose can over-fire on quoted user text. The rule set starts narrow with the done-claim patterns the clean-coder family already defines.

An empty edit journal is its own outcome (no_edits in the ledger), never a silent pass mistaken for verified. Ships in observe (D7).
tasks.risk: Long test suites at Stop time add latency. The verify config carries a per-command timeout and the gate reports elapsed time to the ledger.

stories.user_story: As an operator, I want delegated work held to the same turn-end discipline, so that a subagent cannot hand back unproved claims invisibly.

tasks.detail: New hook mirroring stop.py for the SubagentStop payload (agent_id, agent_type, agent_transcript_path, last_assistant_message). Shares the scan path through the lib helpers (scanner families plus lib/done_claims), imported, never edited, so no file ownership overlaps with E2-S1-T1. Also covers the deterministic half of the SubagentStop QA idea. Closed after two executable critic rounds. Review replaced a single session-wide pending boolean with an atomic per-agent identity set, preventing concurrent subagents from consuming or stealing each other's release proof. Missing IDs use a collision-safe sentinel, corrupt legacy roots fail closed, and tests pin interleaving, repeat cycles, attribution, and parent-state preservation.

stories.title: TaskCompleted gate
stories.user_story: As an operator, I want a task blocked from completing while its changed files carry findings or its verify matrix fails, so that a bad done lands per task, not at turn end.

tasks.title: E2-S3-T1: task_completed.py verification gate
tasks.detail: New hook merging the three TaskCompleted ideas: a discipline scan over the session edit journal's files plus an optional verify-matrix run at task completion, with exit-2 semantics. stories.title: PostToolBatch single-pass scan
stories.user_story: As an operator, I want one coherent block message per parallel edit batch, so that findings across simultaneous writes are deduplicated and cross-file patterns are visible.
acceptance_criteria: record.py's per-call scan stays canonical and is never suppressed or buffered (D13)

batch.py correlates via tool_use_id (payload contract and ledger row field) between the tool_calls array and the batch's PostToolUse rows, and reports only new cross-file findings, so its dedupe is of its own output and nothing is lost if PostToolBatch never fires

tasks.title: E2-S4-T1: batch.py additive cross-file pass (D13)

If the id is absent in live payloads (contract test plus smoke), it degrades to cross-file rules only. record.py is untouched and remains the guaranteed fallback, which is also why this task owns no record.py path. Validation and trust-boundary regressions live in a second test module so both files stay below the scanner's hard 1000-line cap. Closed after executable adversarial review hardened temporal correlation, semantic call identity, stable file identity, malformed exact-shape boundaries, hostile Python protocols, typed memoized DAG canonicalization, and mutation-sensitive race proofs. The accepted residual is per-file stable reads rather than one atomic multi-file snapshot.
tasks.risk: Correlation rests on tool_use_id arriving in both payloads. The degraded mode and the batch-absent case are both explicit tests, so neither assumption can fail silently.

stories.title: Failure-event handling
stories.user_story: As an operator, I want repeated tool failures met with deterministic guidance and unhealthy MCP servers short-circuited, so that the agent neither weakens changes to dodge errors nor burns turns on dead providers.

a streak threshold injects a fix-the-root-cause instruction naming the repeated failure

Event normalization extends the central lib/payloads.py contract per D2; hooks never project raw event keys independently. Hostile-input and parser regressions live in a separate boundary test module so every test file stays below the product scanner's hard 1000-line cap. Closed after executable adversarial review added exact trust-boundary projection, safe session and persistence-root authority, atomic state noninterference, truthful success resets, spec-compatible MCP identities, lexical target canonicalization, and mutation-sensitive concurrency and parser proofs.
tasks.risk: Backoff state is keyed per session first. Cross-session escalation only if the ledger shows need. Fail-safe: if PostToolUseFailure never fires, the health substate stays empty and pre_mcp allows everything, degraded but harmless.

stories.user_story: As an operator, I want edits to linter, formatter, typecheck, hook, and ignore configs and to ADW's own wiring blocked unless explicitly authorized, so the agent cannot green-light checks by weakening the checker.

tasks.title: E10-T0: Live Stop smoke (the MVP experiment)
tasks.detail: Lead-driven live run right after E1 plus E2-S1 plus E2-W-T0 land: the smoke session sets the stop family to enforce in its own .agent-discipline.json (D7 keeps the shipped default at observe), provokes a Stop block, observes the release, confirms the ledger row, and records the installed Claude Code version. Every further wiring task in the graph depends on this passing. A failure here stops the rollout at one hook deep. The two live halves, seeing the Stop block land and seeing the release after the fix, are human observation and deliberately live here in detail rather than in checks. The machine-checkable residue is the checks, and the smoke session is pinned from the client, not from the ledger: the procedure's first step, before provoking the block, is rm -f ~/.agent-discipline/ledger/smoke-session.txt && printf %s "<session_id>" > ~/.agent-discipline/ledger/smoke-session.txt with the session id the client shows, so a skipped write leaves the pin absent and the gate fails closed instead of reading last run's value. The gate then requires, within that session only: a stop block row, with every ledger row required to carry a ts (any row without one fails with a named ledger-corruption message, since E1-S1-T4 always writes ts, so a missing timestamp can never silently weaken a comparison), a first block inside a hardcoded two-hour recency window of the current UTC time, parsed with datetime.fromisoformat and compared as datetimes, never as strings against the clock, and a release row at or after the first block. The two-hour window exists because this gates a live smoke whose evidence should be minutes old: it is generous for a human-paced smoke, and it is what makes historical evidence unable to satisfy a live gate, holding even when the pin step is skipped. A second, distinct staleness guard requires the pinned session to hold the newest row in the whole ledger, any family and any outcome. It exists because recency alone accepts a stale pin naming a session that blocked and released inside the window while the current attempt is stuck, and it catches that whenever the current run wrote anything at all, a lone heartbeat included. The two clauses cover different failures, recency catches old evidence and the newest-row guard catches recent evidence belonging to the wrong run, so neither is redundant and neither may be deleted. Put precisely: recency bounds how old the pinned evidence itself may be, while the any-row check confirms nothing more current exists anywhere in the ledger than what is pinned, and recency does not imply freshness relative to other sessions. Every time comparison in this gate, the staleness guard, the recency window, and the block-to-release ordering, compares instants, never strings: timestamps parse with datetime.fromisoformat, naive treated as UTC, so a timezone-offset ts can neither sort a release above a block it precedes nor let a stale pinned session outrank newer rows from the current one, and a malformed ts raises naming the bad string. The marker semantics still back the comparison, a release row is written only by a passing stop_hook_active retry, which the client sends only after a block. Accepted residual: if the operator skips the pin step and the current run writes no ledger rows at all, a stale pin naming a session still inside the two-hour window can pass, which is why the pin write with rm -f is the first step of the procedure and why the live human observation of the block and the release remains the backstop, this case is bounded by the window and the newest-row guard, not closed. The session also records the client version with claude --version > ~/.agent-discipline/ledger/client-version.txt. Known limitation, accepted by the lead: the test -s check on client-version.txt is a presence check that a stale file from an earlier run can satisfy, it is not session-scoped evidence.
checks: python3 -c 'import glob,json,os,datetime; sid_path=os.path.expanduser("~/.agent-discipline/ledger/smoke-session.txt"); assert os.path.exists(sid_path), "smoke-session.txt missing"; sid=open(sid_path).read().strip(); assert sid, "smoke-session.txt empty"; rows=[json.loads(line) for path in glob.glob(os.path.expanduser("~/.agent-discipline/ledger/")+"*.jsonl") for line in open(path)]; stop_rows=[row for row in rows if row.get("family")=="stop" and row.get("session_id")==sid]; blocks=[row for row in stop_rows if row.get("outcome")=="block"]; releases=[row for row in stop_rows if row.get("outcome")=="release"]; assert blocks, "no stop block row in the recorded smoke session"; assert all(row.get("ts") for row in rows), "ledger row without ts, ledger corruption, E1-S1-T4 always writes ts"; utc=datetime.timezone.utc; norm=lambda value: (lambda parsed: parsed if parsed.tzinfo else parsed.replace(tzinfo=utc))(datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(value)); pinned_all=[row for row in rows if row.get("session_id")==sid]; assert max(norm(row["ts"]) for row in pinned_all)>=max(norm(row["ts"]) for row in rows), "stale smoke-session.txt: another session holds newer ledger rows, re-pin the current smoke session"; first_block=min(norm(row["ts"]) for row in blocks); now=datetime.datetime.now(utc); assert abs(now-first_block)<=datetime.timedelta(hours=2), "stale evidence: the pinned smoke block is outside the two-hour live window"; assert any(norm(row["ts"])>=first_block for row in releases), "no release row at or after the block instant in the recorded smoke session"'

The machine-checkable residue is the checks: every event key wired in the Claude snippet has at least one ledger row within the verification session, pinned by a recorded id rather than inferred from recency: at the start of the live run the lead removes any stale pin and writes the session id shown by the client with rm -f ~/.agent-discipline/ledger/live-session.txt && printf %s "<session_id>" > ~/.agent-discipline/ledger/live-session.txt, so a skipped write leaves the pin absent and the gate fails closed, and the coverage gate reads only that session (run from the repo root so the snippet path resolves). A recency clause requires the pinned session's newest row to sit inside the same hardcoded two-hour window of current UTC time that E10-T0 uses, parsed with datetime.fromisoformat, because live-verification evidence should be minutes old. It is what stops a historical session from satisfying the gate however complete its coverage is, holding even when the pin step is skipped. A second, distinct staleness guard requires the pinned session to hold the newest ledger row overall, catching a within-window stale pin whenever the current run wrote any row at all. Its comparison parses timestamps as instants, naive treated as UTC, exactly like the recency clause, and any ledger row without a ts fails loudly as named corruption so a missing timestamp can never silently weaken the guard. The two clauses cover different failures, so neither is redundant and neither may be deleted. Put precisely: recency bounds how old the pinned evidence itself may be, while the any-row check confirms nothing more current exists anywhere in the ledger than what is pinned, and recency does not imply freshness relative to other sessions. The same bounded residual as E10-T0 applies when the pin step is skipped and the current run writes nothing, and the session writes its results to ~/.agent-discipline/ledger/live-verification-results.md alongside the client version file from E10-T0. Known limitation, accepted by the lead: the test -s checks on live-verification-results.md and client-version.txt are presence checks that stale files from an earlier run can satisfy, they are not session-scoped evidence.

responsibility.system_boundary: Users: agent operators on Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi. Data subjects: authors of the code, prose, prompts, and secrets that pass through hooks. Non-users affected: repo collaborators who receive blocked or gated commits. Operators: the lead, who owns git and the live install.
responsibility.fairness: Rules are content-mechanical (punctuation, structure, sequences), not author-attributed. No per-person profiling. Dead-end and dead-rules stores key on repo and rule, never on user identity.
responsibility.privacy: Prompt text is scanned in-process and never persisted. Session state stores derived flags, not prompt bodies. The dead-end registry lives outside the repo, keyed by repo path. The redaction tier (E7) handles secrets and is opt-in behind a human policy review (E7-H). Notification ideas pushing session activity to public topics (ntfy) are deferred partly on this ground.
responsibility.harm: The chief foreseeable harm is false blocking that halts legitimate work or erases a human prompt. Mitigations: D7 observe-first with adjudicated promotion, D9 inject-first firewall, respect for the documented cap of eight consecutive Stop blocks, and a per-gate kill-switch. The abuse case of an agent weakening its own leash is covered by E4 (tamper seal, ConfigChange defense).
responsibility.carbon: Regex scanning is cheap. Heavyweight repo checks (lint, typecheck, tests) are cached and scoped to touched files. Log-only hooks run async:true so they add no synchronous compute to the turn.
responsibility.monitoring: The findings ledger is reviewed weekly during rollout (validation.decision_rule). After a gate family promotes to default-on, the lead owns an ongoing monthly ledger review for that family, recorded as part of the E10-T2 decision. The dead-rules scorecard identifies the next prose rule worth promoting and gates that never fire (candidates for deletion).

risks.risk: The redaction tier mishandles a secret (misses it, persists it, or stores a dictionary-reversible fingerprint of a low-entropy identifier).
risks.mitigation: E7 is default-off behind human policy review E7-H. The block tier (never-store) handles true secrets. Mapping fingerprints are keyed HMACs under a user-owned key outside the repo (0600, rotation defined at E7-H), so a stolen mapping store cannot be dictionary-reversed without the key.

risks.risk: Dead-end mining heuristics produce noisy false dead ends that misdirect future sessions.
risks.mitigation: E8 ships inject-warn only by default. The PreToolUse block mode is a separate opt-in. Entries carry evidence pointers and expire.

risks.risk: A checked-in .agent-discipline.json in an untrusted repo triggers automatic command execution through the verify or formatter recipes.
risks.mitigation: D12: command-bearing config is inert until the user records a trust grant outside the repo, commands run as argv lists with no shell, and the tamper seal cannot substitute for the grant because it only protects an already-trusted config.

risks.risk: A client version that does not know a newly registered event key rejects the whole settings file before any hook runs, so a bad registration disables ADW entirely instead of no-oping.
risks.mitigation: D14: train-by-train registration behind the Stop smoke, sandbox-HOME install with parse-back and the client's own config validation in every wiring task's checks, a minimum-client-version column in the parity matrix, and timestamped install backups as instant rollback.
